title: A sociotechnical view of algorithmic fairness
abstract: Abstract Algorithmic fairness (AF) has been framed as a newly emerging technology that mitigates systemic discrimination in automated decision‐making, providing opportunities to improve fairness in information systems (IS). However, based on a state‐of‐the‐art literature review, we argue that fairness is an inherently social concept and that technologies for AF should therefore be approached through a sociotechnical lens. We advance the discourse on AF as a sociotechnical phenomenon. Our research objective is to embed AF in the sociotechnical view of IS . Specifically, we elaborate on why outcomes of a system that uses algorithmic means to assure fairness depend on mutual influences between technical and social structures. This perspective can generate new insights that integrate knowledge from both technical fields and social studies. Further, it spurs new directions for IS debates. We contribute as follows: First, we problematize fundamental assumptions in the current discourse on AF based on a systematic analysis of 310 articles. Second, we respond to these assumptions by theorizing AF as a sociotechnical construct. Third, we propose directions for IS researchers to enhance their impacts by pursuing a unique understanding of sociotechnical AF. We call for and undertake a holistic approach to AF. A sociotechnical perspective on AF can yield holistic solutions to systemic biases and discrimination.

claims.text: Algorithmic fairness is an inherently social concept and should be approached through a sociotechnical lens.
The existing literature on algorithmic fairness is dominated by technical perspectives that reduce fairness to a mathematical construct.
It is mathematically impossible to simultaneously fulfill all group-level mathematical definitions of fairness.
Technical approaches to algorithmic fairness predominantly rely on context-independence, time-independence, and component-independence assumptions.
Social perspectives on algorithmic fairness frequently treat technical fairness approaches as a black box without analyzing specific technical operationalizations or trade-offs.
A complex decision system composed of individual fair technical components does not guarantee fair overall sociotechnical outcomes.

limitations.text: Collecting sensitive demographic attributes required by group and individual mathematical fairness notions may be prohibited by legal regulations.
Explainable machine learning techniques frequently generate explanations that are not perceived as useful or practical by human decision-makers.
The literature search process is constrained by the choice of target databases, keyword queries, and inclusion filtering rules.
The summary and synthesis of individual articles in the literature review are necessarily selective and condensed.

future_work.text: Develop frameworks for evaluating and auditing algorithmic fairness solutions in real-world, dynamic organizational contexts rather than relying on synthetic or decontextualized benchmark datasets.
Identify context-dependent requirements for explainable machine learning tailored to specific high-stakes stakeholders such as policy decision-makers, medical auditors, and judicial officers.
Formulate data governance and management practices that ensure fairness while maintaining data consistency, integrity, and security.
Investigate optimal division of labor, joint agency, and interaction patterns within human-algorithm decision-making teams to prevent uncritical automation bias.
Develop system-theoretic approaches to detect, formalize, and mitigate self-reinforcing feedback loops that propagate bias after deployment.

methodologies.description: A systematic multidisciplinary literature review and problematization analysis of 280 articles (166 conference papers and 114 multidisciplinary journal papers) to explicate and challenge core assumptions in algorithmic fairness research.
